5d9fc947-f2a4-45fd-ae3c-c9c3f95e592d.title: The Batman 2: Matt Reeves Officially Reveals Robert Pattinson’s New Look on Batman Day
5d9fc947-f2a4-45fd-ae3c-c9c3f95e592d.incipit: The annual Bat day is here, and we have a new sneak peek of The Batman 2. Matt Reeves, who is helming the sequel, has shared a new look from the film ahead of its 2028 release. This year’s September 19, which...
5d9fc947-f2a4-45fd-ae3c-c9c3f95e592d.body: The annual Bat day is here, and we have a new sneak peek of The Batman 2 . Matt Reeves, who is helming the sequel, has shared a new look from the film ahead of its 2028 release. This year’s September 19, which is celebrated as Batman Day, is significant, as the Robert Pattinson sequel is currently being filmed. Taking to X, Reeves shared a single photo showing a silhouette of the Dark Knight. The moody, cinematic shot does not reveal much. However, it sure adds to the existing excitement to see Pattinson’s Batman back on screen. “Happy Batman Day to everyone from London ,” Reeves wrote in the caption of the photo. Have a look at it here: Reeves is not the only DC director who celebrated Batman Day. Zack Snyder, who directed Batman v Superman and Justice League, shared a photo of Ben Affleck’s Batman, marking the day. James Gunn posted a Sam Kieth artwork from the Batman: Ghost s comic. Gunn is currently filming a Superman sequel with David Corenswet. Robert Pattinson’s Batman Returns With Updated Suit in Matt Reeves’ Sequel Robert Pattinson as Batman | Credit: Warner Bros. Pictures The Batman 2 will feature a more updated Batsuit for Robert Pattinson’s Dark Knight. In July 2026, when Matt Reeves first shared the camera test, it confirmed that the suit is not identical to its 2022 version. A fan also pointed out that the cowl now has longer ears. Reeves himself reposted the observation and confirmed, “You are not crazy.” Screenrant noted that there is some extra protection to the Batsuit, which is a chin guard that was spotted in the test footage. The outlet also claimed that the collars looked higher from the angles available for the suit. French publication Première examined some production photos, identifying a slight modification of the armor plates around the abdomen and torso. However, most of these remain speculations, except the ears of Batman’s cowl, which Reeves himself confirmed. The Batman 2 Picks Up After Gotham Flood Robert Pattinson in The Batman 2 Camera Test Footage | Credit: Warner Bros. Pictures Most of the plot for The Batman 2 is being kept under wraps. The available loglines (via Rotten Tomatoes) reveal that the sequel is set against the backdrop of the winter after the Gotham flood that engulfed the city at the end of the first film. Matt Reeves has revealed that the sequel will go beyond the aftermath of the disaster. He pointed out (via Variety ) that while the first film starring Pattinson is mostly focused on Batman, the sequel will explore more of the man behind the mask, Bruce Wayne. He noted that he “ never wanted to lose ” Pattinson “ at the center of” the origin stories. “ That is really what we set our aim on, ” Reeves added. The core trio of Robert Pattinson, Jeffrey Wright, and Andy Serkis will be returning in the sequel, along with Colin Farrell, Jayme Lawson, and Gil Perez-Abraham. The new casting roster includes Scarlett Johansson, Sebastian Stan, Charles Dance, and Sebastian Koch. The Batman 2 is now set for a February 18, 2028 theatrical release. What did you notice in the new look shared by Matt Reeves? Tell us in the comments.

68b7b805-8134-413f-8861-0d9dabc228c3.title: Sure, it has ‘Star Wars,’ but the Lucas Museum’s free library and gardens are just as stellar
68b7b805-8134-413f-8861-0d9dabc228c3.incipit: Two of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s most unique and transportive spaces don’t require a paid admission ticket.Written by Michael JulianoNational Things to Do Editor, U.S.Saturday September 19...
68b7b805-8134-413f-8861-0d9dabc228c3.body: Two of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s most unique and transportive spaces don’t require a paid admission ticket. Written by Michael Juliano National Things to Do Editor, U.S. Saturday September 19 2026 Share Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out | Library at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art You’ve probably already seen footage of the Star Wars props, the Van Gogh–inspired Pikachu and the striking spaceship-like architecture. But the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s most unique assets actually might be outside of the galleries—and, after it officially debuts on September 22, open to visitors for free, no museum ticket required. George Lucas has referred to his eponymous institution as a temple to the people’s art, where a self-portrait of Frida Kahlo, an oil painting of dogs playing poker and a screen-used Batman suit make unexpected neighbors. But that for-the-people perspective also— especially —extends to the entrancing gardens surrounding the building, as well as the open-to-the-public library . “I love that if you walk into our parks and gardens, you feel different,” says Lucas Museum CEO Tracey Bates. “You do feel like you’ve been transported somewhere else, which is the joy of storytelling—which is what the museum is all about.” Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Whether you enter down the street from the Metro station on Vermont Avenue, across from the Natural History Museum and Coliseum at Bill Robertson Lane or into the middle of the Exposition Park –adjacent campus via the parking garage, you’ll find yourself in a mix of open grassy spaces and meandering walking paths. (Access here is completely separate from the museum galleries, which cost $25 for adults and nothing for kids 17 and under.) Dense clusters of native flora that’ve been maturing off-site for the past six years add much-needed greenery to what was once a parking lot. The cloud-shaped profile of the museum building, designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects, seems to float above the multi-tiered gardens. Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Sculpture of Leia strangling Jabba the Hutt at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art And then there’s the bronze statue of Jabba the Hutt—being strangled by a shackle-wielding Leia. And Padmé fighting off a pillar-climbing nexu à la Attack of the Clones . Or a fountain topped with Yoda and his post-Disney-acquisition counterpart, Grogu. Star Wars may only represent 7% of the museum’s displays, but it’s well represented in the gardens. It’s not the only art on display, though: You’ll also find, among other pieces, sculptures of Rosie the Riveter, King Kong stop-motion animator Willis O’Brien and Terracotta Daughters , artist Prune Nourry’s response to China’s famous Terracotta Army. The free-to-visit park space, designed by Mia Lehrer and the team at Studio-MLA, also boasts a shallow amphitheater along its southern end. Though the full slate of programming is still to come, Bates expects that once a month on either Friday or Saturday (when the museum is open until 9pm), there’ll be a relatively large activation in the amphitheater (either for free or via accessibly priced tickets). Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Yoda and Grogu sculpture at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art But you don’t need a formal event to unwind in the garden: Bates invites people to come on their way home from school, before an LAFC match, to sit down and sketch, or for a meal at a picnic table after a visit to the California Science Center . “We want it to become part of their daily lives almost,” she says. “I just want people to feel safe, relaxed, and I’d love to inspire creativity here because that’s what George would want.” Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Library at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Speaking of creativity, the library here just might be the most imaginative space in the entire campus. Research libraries may typically give off a stuffy, studious air, but that’s certainly not the case at the Lucas Museum’s library, where light streams through the building’s spaceship-like shell and into a warm, Arts and Crafts–style sitting area with three floors of shelves carrying art books on everything from paleoart to Renaissance warfare to rock & roll posters. It’s an all-encompassing collection that library director Joan Jocson-Singh hopes will draw in all walks of visitors—and the free admission is certainly a strong incentive too. “The fact that we’re open to the community and that you don’t need to pay for a museum ticket really, I think, dismantles the notion that libraries are for a specific type of person,” she says. You’re welcome to peruse any of the books on the first-floor shelves and sit and linger as you read through them. (The library opens the same time as the museum and closes an hour earlier; just mention you’re headed there at the security checkpoint, look for the Naboo starfighter in the main plaza’s south building and then head up to the circulation desk.) Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art The collection started when the museum’s curators began researching some of the works that would ultimately go on display in the main galleries; these first-floor shelves mirror those themes, with books on comics, illustration and graphic arts, among other topics, and everything from Norman Rockwell to Dungeons & Dragons to the Separate Cinema Archive of early Black filmmaking. Spot any books with their covers facing out and they’re likely some of Jocson-Singh’s favorites, whether that’s a primer on Hollywood portrait photographers, a collection of He-Man illustrations or a celebration of Babar. And over on the tables, you’ll spot what she refers to as, well, table books: heavy, oversized Taschen editions that are typically kept behind a shop counter, but here they’re out in the open with X-Men comics, Donald Duck drawings or the sci-fi and fantasy works of Frank Frazetta. “Some of these books are out of print and rare,” Jocson-Singh says. “But it also gives you insight into our founders [George Lucas and Mellody Hobson]; you’re learning about the art that’s in the galleries that may not have titles that circulate widely, and it’s pretty unique because this museum is legitimizing and, what I like to say, academicizing art that hasn’t had a home before.” Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Library at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Though the mezzanine and third-floor shelves are off limits to the public, they’re filled with fascinating collections for researchers: titles about military history, vehicles, the occult, adventuring and Americana gifted straight from Lucas and Hobson’s personal collection at Skywalker Ranch (the museum shelves are even styled as an homage to that private library), as well as volumes on major art movements like modernism, cubism and Canadian landscape art that have been donated by Steve Martin. (Some museum-loving Angelenos may remember that the comedy icon curated an exhibition on that latter topic at the Hammer Museum about a decade ago.) All of the books in the library are non-circulating (so you can’t take them out of the room), and once you’re done reading, don’t bother trying to place them back on the shelves yourself: A bright orange book trolley with a photo of Yoda reminds you, “Reshelve, do not. Leave books here, you must!” You can expect to find a full catalog to browse on the museum’s website following the September 22 opening. For Jocson-Singh, that day is likely to be a pretty monumental moment. “The first time we started doing previews and had people in the space... seeing children come in and light up,” she says. “To see adults come in here and look at books that they had such invested interest in that you typically don’t see in a museum library just felt so rewarding.” Been there, done that? 0f912d98-0052-463f-a290-a18c3102f667.title: 5 Reasons to Watch The 2026 Resident Evil Film - Abstract AF!
0f912d98-0052-463f-a290-a18c3102f667.incipit: Bryan (Austin Abrams) just wants to deliver a package. Unfortunately, the address is in Raccoon City. Things get increasingly ridiculous from there. Here are six reasons to watch Resident Evil. #ResidentEvil #Horror #HorrorMovies
0f912d98-0052-463f-a290-a18c3102f667.body: There are plenty of reasons to watch the 2026 Resident Evil film, but I’m obviously not going to waste one of them on “watch it if you’re a fan of the franchise.” Fans are going to watch it anyway; they don’t need some stranger on the internet telling them to. And yes, the film is packed with references and Easter eggs from the games, so there’s plenty here for longtime fans to enjoy. Although it’s like a side-quest, so it’s easy for some to find it lacking the tension and grit of an apocalyptic survival story. Anyway, with the most obvious reason out of the way, here are six slightly more useful ones: 1. It basically plays like a Resident Evil game Watch it if you’re up for a game-like horror story that’s surprisingly comical in tone. A lot of sequences are shot almost like you’re watching someone stream a Resident Evil game, complete with moments that feel straight out of a first-person shooter set-up. I really wasn’t expecting it to unfold like a horror-comedy, especially since most of the older Resident Evil stuff I’ve watched has been seriously dystopian and oppressive. But those who aren’t fans of the horror-comedy genre might go ‘what the hell?!’. Click here for a longer review or listen to a short audio version below. 2. It’s from the director of Weapons If you loved Weapons , there’s another reason to check this out: Zach Cregger is back in the director’s chair and shares the writing credit with Shay Hatten, who has worked on the John Wick films. Just don’t expect the complexity or wickedness of Weapons . Resident Evil is a much more straightforward tale about a delivery guy trying to get something to a hospital in Raccoon City while everything around him goes spectacularly wrong. 3. The story is refreshingly simple Honestly, this is also part of the appeal. There’s no need to keep track of a dozen characters or an elaborate conspiracy. The story is told largely from the POV of one random courier driving towards Raccoon City on a snowy night. He gets into an accident on a deserted stretch of road, and things just keep going downhill from there. Yet despite all the increasingly horrid things that happen to him, the poor guy remains bizarrely committed to making his delivery. 4. Austin Abrams gives you someone you actually want to survive Austin Abrams as Bryan is the absolute heart of the film, and you genuinely want him to succeed even when his odds of survival seem to be about 10%. That’s always a plus in horror, because there are definitely movies where the protagonist becomes so annoying that you start rooting for the monster instead. I couldn’t immediately remember an example, but apparently I wished exactly that upon the protagonist of the 2022 Resident Evil series . I know this only because I reread my old review today while hyperlinking it to this one. So... thanks, past me. 5. Logic happily takes a back seat to gross, wacky horror If you’re absolutely chill with horror movies sacrificing logic in the name of some wild-as-hell gore, Resident Evil keeps delivering. There are plenty of wacky monsters, gross transformations and sequences that make you wonder what exactly you’re watching. And obviously, someone puking their guts out all over the protagonist is practically mandatory gross-out horror at this point. 6. It’s a crisp 90 minutes Finally, Resident Evil knows when to get out. The ending feels abrupt, but at least the filmmakers don’t stretch things out or suddenly get overly sentimental. Any longer and the film probably would’ve started becoming overbearing. We watched it in a theatre, where there was no magical fast-forward button, and not once did I wish I had one. For a 90-minute horror movie, that’s a pretty solid compliment. 9c2b3fa5-1f17-438e-b48b-e6a19b4c627e.title: Jennifer Lawrence to Lead “The Flood”, Director Zach Cregger’s Follow-Up to “Resident Evil”
9c2b3fa5-1f17-438e-b48b-e6a19b4c627e.incipit: Jennifer Lawrence has joined an original movie from Zach Cregger set for a 2028 release, the studio confirmed on Tuesday, Sept. 29Sci-fi thriller The Flood will be Cregger's next project following...
9c2b3fa5-1f17-438e-b48b-e6a19b4c627e.body: Jennifer Lawrence has joined an original movie from Zach Cregger set for a 2028 release, the studio confirmed on Tuesday, Sept. 29 Sci-fi thriller The Flood will be Cregger's next project following the release of horror hit Resident Evil "Jennifer is one of a kind, and I'm beyond excited to see her in this role," said the filmmaker Jennifer Lawrence is gearing up for her next big screen role. The Oscar winner, 36, has joined The Flood , the next project from horror hitmaker Zach Cregger , per a New Line Cinema release shared with PEOPLE on Tuesday, Sept. 29. Written, directed and produced by Cregger, 45, the original sci-fi thriller from Warner Bros., New Line Cinema and production companies Amblin Entertainment and Vertical Entertainment is set for an Aug. 11, 2028 release. Jennifer Lawrence; Zach Cregger Credit: Karwai Tang/WireImage; Rick Kern/Getty The news comes fresh off the theatrical release of Cregger's Resident Evil , another adaptation in the video game-inspired franchise. Released Sept. 18 and starring Austin Abrams , the box office hit continues the filmmaker's stretch of buzzy horror titles, from 2022's Barbarian to 2025's Oscar-winning Weapons . In a statement included in the release, Cregger praised Warner Bros. and New Line Cinema as "an absolute dream to collaborate with on Weapons , and I couldn't be happier to dive in with them again. Jennifer is one of a kind, and I'm beyond excited to see her in this role." Lawrence has continued to star in movie roles while expanding her work as a producer under the company Excellent Cadaver. After leading last year's Die My Love , she will reportedly reprise her role as Katniss Everdeen in the new Hunger Games prequel Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters Nov. 20) and appear in the Martin Scorsese thriller What Happens at Night . The mother of two has also discussed developing a movie about Miss Piggy alongside fellow producer and friend Emma Stone , with Oh, Mary! writer-star Cole Escola as its screenwriter. 4cf2c1c0-74ff-4347-b7bc-79ac7ff4dd0d.title: John Wilson 'History of Concrete' Interview: Kim Kardashian and More
4cf2c1c0-74ff-4347-b7bc-79ac7ff4dd0d.incipit: John Wilson’s new documentary “The History of Concrete” is, of course, about the history of concrete. But...
4cf2c1c0-74ff-4347-b7bc-79ac7ff4dd0d.body: SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “ The History of Concrete ,” now in theaters. John Wilson’s new documentary “The History of Concrete” is, of course, about the history of concrete. But it’s also about selling a documentary titled “The History of Concrete,” which, it turns out, is almost as hard as concrete. It sees the filmmaker, best known for his HBO series “How To,” traveling across the world — to concrete conventions in Las Vegas and New Orleans, to ancient buildings in Italy and to graves in undisclosed locations. But he also documents the Zoom meetings in between, where he pitches the idea to Hollywood executives and tells them the film’s title. Underneath their deep sighs, you can almost hear them mutter: Who wants to watch a movie called “The History of Concrete”? “I genuinely did want to make the definitive movie about concrete,” Wilson says of the doc, now in theaters via Magnolia Pictures. “I ended up incorporating the meta aspects about a year or so into the process, because I felt like that was becoming a more interesting story. And I wanted to make something that another filmmaker could learn something from, about how things are produced, because that was always a mystery to me growing up.” Of course, it’s not all slabs of rock. Wilson finds humanity in the cracks of “The History of Concrete,” letting his camera guide him toward a professional “gum buster,” a grieving local musician and dozens of other fascinating characters. It is perhaps the filmmaker’s most substantial — and heart-forward — work to date. “The History of Concrete” by John Wilson John Wilson In the film, as you’re struggling to sell said film, I kept thinking: It’s John Wilson, obviously he’s not going to make a boring movie about concrete! It doesn’t matter. In terms of the money, we were asking for what a Netflix documentary would cost. Our budget ask was also scaled to what “How To” would cost, so I didn’t think we were being that outrageous. The struggle is actually a lot more real than what’s on screen in the film. I just didn’t want to weigh it down with more struggle. People laugh when they hear the title, but you laugh knowing that the movie is done. It’s a lot different when someone is asking you directly for money to make this thing that doesn’t exist yet. Would you give your own money to make “The History of Concrete”? Even if it’s me, I don’t know. It’s a strange proposition. The documentary space has mutated slightly, and I think people value the wrong things a lot of the time. That’s what I wanted to comment on, in a way. What are the things people value? People are focused on retelling stories that have already happened — whether it’s a triple homicide or a musician who has gone through all the motions of their career. Certain people with money have a hard time with imagination and this idea of art-making for the sake of it. You need to go through several layers of approval. I didn’t realize how hard it was going to be. Structurally, the film is similar to “How To.” Was working in the feature-length format freeing or more challenging? It was freeing in that I was able to have more durational subjects — like the 3,100-mile race that takes place over the course of a few months. I don’t know if I would have been able to cover that as substantially in an episode of the show. Same with one of the main characters I spent a lot of time with near the end of the film. I spent a year and a half with him, and I wouldn’t have been able to do that without the elasticity of a feature film. But emotionally, it is a little different than the show, and while superficially it shares a lot of the same qualities, I set out to make something that was much broader in scope and almost felt like a prequel to the show, because it’s kind of the foundation on which the rest of the work was built. The subject of the film is literally our foundation. I found it notable that you chose to explore concrete, a hard topic, in a physical sense, but you can’t help but be led to the softness — the humanity. Yeah, and Jack, the musician I spent a lot of time with, has the softest heart of all. In the world of hard surfaces, he’s got a really soft interior. How do you view your responsibility to these subjects, specifically him? Do you approach it as a journalist? Do you have an ongoing relationship with him outside of the film? I met him at a liquor store right next to my house, so he’s the kind of person I’d see all the time. So in that case, I treated it as if he’s someone I’m going to see frequently. But also, my friend Francis Carr, who was one of my producers, would mostly correspond with Jack whenever he was going to have a show or something like that. There was a bit of distance — it wasn’t just him and me. I think there’s some value to a certain level of journalistic distance when making something like this, just because I’m dealing with so many people at the same time. Has he seen the film? I think he saw part of it in the Rockaways. But he was rehearsing, because he was playing the after party next door during the screening, so he couldn’t fully watch it. He’s going to be at one of the premieres at IFC over the weekend. I expect that one of the most talked-about moments of the film will be the Kim Kardashian scene. You’re at a GQ dinner and filming Dwyane Wade as he gives a toast to Kim, and she’s looking right into your camera. It’s all very unsettling. How uncomfortable was that to film? The discomfort started when I entered the room, and the filming only eased that discomfort. I had just never seen an uninterrupted shot of Kim Kardashian before, and I knew this was going to be the only chance for me to get it. I wasn’t pursuing it, but I thought it was a very rare environment, and there’s something very awkward and strange about these celebrity events. I wanted to capture that somehow by not including any score and just letting the moment play out, so you have a POV of what it’s like to be sitting across from someone like that at dinner. Did you have any interaction with her at all? No. So how does that work? Were you nervous about putting her in the film? Do you expect to hear from her? It’s a miracle that this film exists and is being released as is — that’s what I’ll say. It was an event that was being documented by someone else too, an internal magazine film-and-photo team. I have no idea where that kind of stuff ends up, but I know it won’t be treated anywhere near how I would treat it. So I think that’s how the footage is able to be in the movie, because it was an event that was captured by someone else as well. But I don’t know where that material will ever end up. The shot of Tim Robinson got the biggest laugh of the entire film at the screening I was at. Were you expecting that to be such a punchline? No. Originally we did not have Tim at the end of that shot, because we just wanted you to sit with the strangeness of that eye-contact moment I was having with Kim. We ended up putting the Tim thing in just because it performed really well when we showed it to people, and I realized comedically you needed something to pop that tension bubble. I love reveals that someone else has been there the whole time. I showed the film internationally in a couple of places, and that shot was crickets. There are some places in the world that don’t know Tim in the same way people do here — same with Hallmark and Chef Boyardee. They don’t know what that stuff is. Is there one shot in the movie you’re proudest of? The shot I really liked a lot was when I’m filming the sidewalk and you see my shadow, but then I’m zooming into the sidewalk, and the light changes really dramatically around me, and my shadow just disappears into the sidewalk. It happened randomly, and it felt very poetic in a way that I didn’t really plan. But on top of that, I think my favorite shot is when the tattoo preservation guy asks his dad where Chef Boyardee is buried. The timing of that was just incredible, and how casual he was. It turned out to be your kicker! I remember trying to figure out what the last shot of the movie should be when I was talking to [producers] Josh [Safdie] and Ronnie [Bronstein] and Eli [Bush]. I was thinking about going to Chef Boyardee’s grave, but we had to have the movie ready in four days, and I didn’t know how I was going to get it. They said, “You have to get that shot,” so I went and shot it by myself on Christmas Eve, which was the day before we locked the movie. So now I know where Chef Boyardee’s grave is. Wow, that’s fascinating that the final shot was so last-minute. It was because we got into Sundance as I was still filming the movie. But it also kind of ties in with the Christmas theme of it all, even though you would never know I filmed that on Christmas Eve.

8c252606-cfa6-481e-9944-bb389ea100fc.title: Henry Winkler Reveals Why His Name Was Cut From 'Scream' Movie Poster
8c252606-cfa6-481e-9944-bb389ea100fc.incipit: Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “Scream” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler’s happier days. The “Happy Days” star played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original “Scream” film, which went on to...
8c252606-cfa6-481e-9944-bb389ea100fc.body: Finding out his name wouldn’t be used on the “ Scream ” poster wasn’t one of Henry Winkler ’s happier days. The “ Happy Days ” star played Principal Arthur Himbry in the original “Scream” film, which went on to become one of the most successful horror franchises. But despite his character’s entrance receiving applause during screen tests for the 1996 movie, Winkler revealed the studio refused to put his name on the poster. “The studio comes to me and says, ‘We can’t put your name on the film. We cannot put you anywhere near the poster,’” Winkler said in an interview for “In Depth With Graham Besinger.” When he asked why, the studio said, “Well, you were the Fonz, and you will knock the balance of horror off if we let them know you’re in it.” Although it left him feeling “insulted,” the actor didn’t overtly protest the studio’s decision. “I said, ‘OK. What can I do?’ I went home upset,” the actor said. “I was bewildered a little bit.” He later learned the same people who had informed him his name wouldn’t be used on the poster were also the ones who asked him if he would do press for the film’s release. Winkler ultimately agreed, noting he obliged for himself, director Wes Craven and the movie as a whole. Now, looking back 30 years later, Winkler said the experience taught him to navigate the unknown. “That’s the lesson. You just show up,” he said, also pointing out that “you have no idea what’s going to happen, but that’s out of your control.” “Scream” also starred Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, David Arquette, Drew Barrymore and Matthew Lillard. The franchise’s latest film, “Scream 7,” became the highest-grossing installment with $176.9 million.

f476383e-a527-4895-b788-53530f697269.title: Narnia’s New Movie Prequel Avoids The Biggest Issue With Film Prequels
f476383e-a527-4895-b788-53530f697269.incipit: Narnia 's upcoming movie prequel Narnia: The Magician's Nephew has already had several details revealed
f476383e-a527-4895-b788-53530f697269.body: Narnia 's upcoming movie prequel Narnia: The Magician's Nephew has already had several details revealed about it that help it avoid one of the most common pitfalls of prequel films made for already popular movie series, since it would be easy to simply follow the prior live-action movies closely in terms of things like visuals and tone. Over the past years, prequel movies following up on major franchises have become an increasingly common aspect of the film world. Captain Marvel provided an MCU prequel origin story set well before almost every other movie in the series released before it, the Wicked movies serve as prequels to The Wizard Of Oz 's story, and films like Cruella and the Minions series have rounded out this slate, ensuring audiences can see what happened before the start of some of their favorite film stories. Narnia is continuing this trend with Narnia: The Magician's Nephew , which is due to be set long before the main events in the fantasy world that audiences saw on-screen years prior. This makes it the more interesting already, especially given how it sounds as though the film is taking a promising approach when it comes to the matter of how to handle being a prequel that follows up on a series with popular pre-existing films. Narnia: The Magician's Nephew Already Is Set Up To Be Very Different To The Main Movies Several years after the last film in the main live-action Narnia movies - which ran from 2005-2010, and ended with The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage Of The Dawn Treader - a new film that adapts the wider book series is on the horizon. As the name Narnia: The Magician's Nephew suggests, the upcoming fantasy movie is set to adapt The Magician's Nephew book, which serves as a prequel of sorts for the Narnia series, though it was released sixth out of the central seven novels. The Magician's Nephew focuses on its two child protagonists learning about other worlds, revealing Narnia is just out of many other universes of sorts. Importantly, The Magician's Nephew also features the lion Aslan constructing Narnia, and explains how the magical wardrobe of The Lion, The Witch, and the Wardrobe fame comes to be, serving as an origin story that explains many crucial corners of the series and its lore. While this means Narnia: The Magician's Nephew will also focus on some of the same characters and settings introduced in the original live-action series, director Greta Gerwig has already confirmed her intention to make the prequel movie very, very different to these films. This is both in that Meryl Streep has been cast as Aslan, and in that she describes her vision for the movie in an interview with Empire to be that of a " rock opera ", which is certainly a very different sounding description to anything that would generally be used to describe the other Narnia movies. Why Narnia: The Magician's Nephew Being Different To The Main Movies Is Good For The Origin Story Prequel Image via MovieStillsDB Though there is something to be said for mainline movies in some series having the same visuals and narrative tone, the wider Narnia series wouldn't seem to benefit from Narnia: The Magician's Nephew being exactly the same as its predecessors. Ultimately, it makes a lot of sense to have the prequel feel different for a range of reasons. Much like the book, it seems the movie adaptation is due to be set decades before the Pevensie family travel to Narnia, meaning keeping things as clearly different as possible helps audiences to register that this story is set way before the one they're likely most familiar with. Similarly, having the franchise take an over a decade break in this sense before having a release that feels exactly the same would arguably be something of a waste, and risks falling into some of the more commonly criticized territory prequel films that release later down the line often fall into in terms of not feeling like their own thing or being willing to take their own risks. Given the directorial history of Greta Gerwig, taking a different approach and letting Narnia: The Magician's Nephew spread its own proverbial wings already sounds like the best movie for the film and wider Narnia series, as Barbie alone strongly supports the idea that Gerwig can take a pre-existing franchise and depict it in a striking way that still feels familiar.

44309c89-00eb-4a30-a53f-fbc8298e08f2.title: This Year's Best New Period Drama Officially Returns In 3 Months
44309c89-00eb-4a30-a53f-fbc8298e08f2.incipit: This year's best and most surprising period drama is officially set to return in just three months
44309c89-00eb-4a30-a53f-fbc8298e08f2.body: This year's best and most surprising period drama is officially set to return in just three months. With massive shows like Bridgerton , The Buccaneers , and The Gilded Age dominating the period drama genre on the small screen, it's hard for newer, smaller shows to make waves. And yet, one unlikely BBC and BritBox Regency-era dramedy did just that, moving away from its competitors' exciting, dramatic (and steamy) romantic entanglements in favor of a warm, sweet, heartfelt, and genuinely funny journey of self-discovery and acceptance. Based on Janice Hadlow's bestselling, Jane Austen-inspired Pride and Prejudice "sequel," The Other Bennet Sister is one of this decade's most refreshing and moving period dramas. Rather than following beloved literary icon Lizzie Bennet, the story focuses on her dismissed middle sister, Mary (played with disarming charm by Call the Midwife' s Ella Bruccoleri), as she distances herself from Longbourn and her overbearing mother to find her place in a world that values marriage and social standing over personal fulfillment. The 10-episode series, which premiered on the BBC and BritBox earlier this year, united viewers and reviewers. The show boasts a near-perfect 98% critics' score and a mightily impressive 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. The Other Bennet Sister also drove five times more new subscribers to BritBox in its first three months on the platform than any other newly launched original series, with nearly half of all subscribers watching the show during that same period. Thankfully, though the series ended on an undeniable high note, covering the entirety of Hadlow's original novel, the show is confirmed to return for three more episodes this holiday season (based on the author's own ideas and written by Sarah Quintrell, who wrote the majority of the show's first 10 episodes), as Mary and her closest friends and family celebrate the holidays in true, comforting Other Bennet Sister -style. The Other Bennet Sister Is The Ultimate Pride & Prejudice Spinoff Photographer: James Pardon - Courtesy of BritBox It's hard to imagine a better sequel or spinoff for Jane Austen's seminal novel, Pride and Prejudice . Rather than copying Austen's style, Hadlow's and Quintrell's adaptation instead puts its own unique, comedic spin on the Bennet family's experiences. The first hour or so covers the events of Pride and Prejudice from Mary's point of view, as audiences learn how her mother's cruelty and standing in her sisters' shadows have shaped her view of the world. After that, as Mary leaves to stay with her much more loving uncle and his wife in London, she discovers a new side of herself: playful, determined, and witty, charming not one but two wholly eligible bachelors with her sincere personality and newfound zest for life. Crucially, though, the show never lets the love triangle get in the way of Mary's individual development. It is, first and foremost, her story. The romance, while undeniably sweet and memorable, isn't everything. The show honors Austen's most important themes while offering viewers a wholly new experience, too. The Other Bennet Sister's Holiday Return Is Perfect For The Show Credit: Bad Wolf/James Pardon, Courtesy of BritBox The Other Bennet Sister 's atmosphere, tone, and themes suit a holiday special. A cozy, heartfelt Christmas story will fit in well with the rest of the series, as Mary settles into her new life and runs her own household while figuring out what she wants her future to look like. Joining Bruccoleri for the festivities are returning stars Dónal Finn as Tom Hayward, Ruth Jones as Mrs. Bennet, Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley, Laurie Davidson as Mr. Ryder, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, and Varada Sethu as Mary's friend, Ann Baxter. Making the show's return a three-part special removes some of the pressure of producing a full second season. It will be a low-stakes chance to catch up with the characters, rather than forcing them into more dramatic situations to up the tension and fill another ten 30-minute episodes. The Other Bennet Sister is incredibly enjoyable as is, but these new holiday episodes are still a most welcome addition to this year's best new period drama. The Other Bennet Sister' s Christmas special premieres this holiday season on BritBox. All other episodes are available to stream now. Release Date May 6, 2026 Network BBC One Directors Jennifer Sheridan Writers Sarah Quintrell, Maddie Dai Cast Ella Bruccoleri Mary Bennet Richard E. Grant Mr. Bennet Creator(s) Janice Hadlow

d7b5c1b5-65bd-45b4-99ae-46de47271b73.title: Cult-Classic PS3, Xbox 360 Game Getting New Sequel After 14 Years
d7b5c1b5-65bd-45b4-99ae-46de47271b73.incipit: A cult-classic game that originally launched on PS3 and Xbox 360 platforms has been confirmed to be getting a new sequel after 14 years. In the last full year of the PS3 and Xbox 360 generation, a number of...
d7b5c1b5-65bd-45b4-99ae-46de47271b73.body: A cult-classic game that originally launched on PS3 and Xbox 360 platforms has been confirmed to be getting a new sequel after 14 years. In the last full year of the PS3 and Xbox 360 generation, a number of iconic games came to each platform. Titles such as Borderlands 2 , Far Cry 3 , Mass Effect 3 , Dishonored , Telltale’s The Walking Dead , and Assassin’s Creed 3 came to both consoles in 2012, alongside countless others. Now, one beloved action game that also launched in this same year is set to make a return on modern hardware with a sequel that many have been clamoring to see for quite some time. Announced this week by Dragami Games to coincide with TGS 2026, the publisher revealed that it’s now developing a sequel to Lollipop Chainsaw . Originally developed by Grasshopper Manufacture, Lollipop Chainsaw released in June 2012 to somewhat middling reviews from critics. However, the game’s outlandish concept that sees a high school cheerleader taking on hordes of zombies while equipped with a chainsaw ended up being quite popular with fans, resulting in Lollipop Chainsaw becoming a cult-classic. As for this long-awaited sequel, the game is officially titled Lollipop Chainsaw 2: Back2Back . Details on this follow-up are still pretty slim, but Dragami Games did share some in-development footage of the project (which you can view below) to give fans an idea of what to expect. Based on this gameplay, Lollipop Chainsaw 2 is still very early in its creation, which means that it could be pretty far down the road, even if Dragami is claiming it’ll be out in 2027. Still, the fact that it’s being made at all is equal parts surprising and exciting. Don’t Get Too Excited About This Sequel Just Yet If there is one concern to have with Lollipop Chainsaw 2 , it’s that the game isn’t being made by the team behind the original. While Dragami Games did work on the remastered version of the first entry, officially titled Lollipop Chainsaw RePOP , Grasshopper Manufacture isn’t involved whatsoever. This is a pretty major deal, especially considering that Grasshopper’s iconic director, Goichi “Suda51” Suda, was the creative lead behind Lollipop Chainsaw . In addition, famed writer/director James Gunn, who happened to co-write the original Lollipop Chainsaw , isn’t involved whatsoever with this sequel. This shouldn’t be a shock in the slightest given that Gunn is now the head of DC Studios, but it’s yet another reason to have doubts about this new installment since so many of the creators behind the original have nothing to do with it this time around. As mentioned, Dragami Games is currently claiming that Lollipop Chainsaw 2 will be out next year, but we’ll see if this ends up holding true. Whenever we learn more about the game, we’ll be sure to update you here on ComicBook .

b126f7ba-9e7f-4da3-bbd9-9f37a95451ff.title: How Deep Is Your Love review – under the sea at Earth’s last frontier with the Psychedelic Elvis Worm
b126f7ba-9e7f-4da3-bbd9-9f37a95451ff.incipit: For the marine biologists in this whimsical eco-documentary, the answer is about 5000 metres down. In the lab, we watch them observing, describing, and classifying the bonkers-looking creatures that survive...
b126f7ba-9e7f-4da3-bbd9-9f37a95451ff.body: F or the marine biologists in this whimsical eco-documentary, the answer is about 5000 metres down. In the lab, we watch them observing, describing, and classifying the bonkers-looking creatures that survive in the freezing-cold waters of the deep sea: blobby little sea pigs and alien glow-in-the-dark sea cucumbers. It seems 90% of life in the deep sea has yet to be named, explains film-maker Eleanor Mortimer in her quirky voiceover. It is the last frontier of exploration on Earth. Mortimer accompanies a team of scientists on an expedition to the eastern Pacific. It takes the ship’s robot four hours to descend the four kilometres to the ocean floor where it trundles along, grabber claw at the ready. A biologist explains that 80% of what they bring up to the surface is new to science. And one of the film’s pleasures is watching the wonderstruck awe on their faces as they clap eyes on never-before-seen creatures. The process of acquiring a Latin name for a new discovery can take years, so in the meantime scientists give them excellent temporary names like the Headless Chicken Monster and the Psychedelic Elvis Worm. In truth, it’s a niche-feeling film, gentle and playfully curious, but an environmental story lurks beneath: deep sea mining. The ocean floor is covered in nodules – lumps the size of baked potatoes – that are rich in metals and minerals. They take millions of years to form, and significantly less time to mine. We listen in to a frustrating debate at the International Seabed Authority about whether mining should be permitted. How high this new eco-worry should rank on the spreadsheet of doom and gloom is as yet unknown. The environmental impact of mining is not yet established. But add it to the list.
